  "title": "Beyond Blocking: Benchmarking and Training Agent Task Recovery After Guardrail Interventions in Multi-Step Tool Use",
  "core_problem": "Current guardrails achieve high unsafe-action blocking rates (up to 94%), but agents almost never recover to complete tasks safely afterward — the safe success rate remains below 5% even when blocking succeeds (The Verifier Tax, 2026). This represents a distinct and underexplored failure mode: post-blocking task recovery. Unlike post-harm recovery (BackBench) where harm has occurred and must be remediated, or post-incident response (AIR) where the system detects and contains safety breaches, post-blocking recovery involves an agent that has been correctly prevented from taking an unsafe action but cannot find an alternative safe path to complete the user's legitimate task. No existing benchmark isolates this specific failure mode, and no training method specifically targets the agent's adaptive replanning ability after correct guardrail intervention.",
  "opportunity": "The Verifier Tax (Mar 2026) quantifies a devastating Safety-Capability Gap: even with 94% unsafe action blocking, safe success rates remain below 5% in tau-bench Airline and Retail domains. This gap is distinct from what AIR (>90% remediation success in post-incident response) and BackBench (50 post-harm recovery scenarios in OSWorld) address. In post-blocking recovery, the guardrail works as intended — harm is prevented — but the agent fails at adaptive replanning. Canonical Path Deviation (Feb 2026) explains the structural difficulty: off-canonical actions compound subsequent deviation by 22.7 percentage points, meaning that once an agent is pushed off its solution path by a blocked action, the probability of finding an alternative path drops sharply. Meanwhile, ToolSafe (Jan 2026) shows that safety-feedback-driven reasoning can improve benign task completion by ~10% and reduce harmful tool invocations by 65%, but this represents pre-execution guidance, not post-blocking recovery training. TraceSafe (Apr 2026) demonstrates that guardrail efficacy in multi-step settings depends more on structural data competence than semantic safety alignment, suggesting the recovery problem requires structured training beyond alignment alone. The recent explosion of turn-level RL methods for multi-step agents (Fission-GRPO, TTPO, T2PO, GAGPO, RC-GRPO) provides mature methodological foundations for training recovery behavior that did not exist even 6 months ago.",
  "landscape": "We identify four distinct recovery paradigms in current agent safety research, each requiring different metrics, training approaches, and benchmarks: (1) POST-BLOCKING TASK RECOVERY (ours): After a guardrail correctly blocks an unsafe action, the agent must find an alternative safe path to complete the original task. The Verifier Tax (Mar 2026) documents <5% safe success rates despite 94% blocking across tau-bench using GPT-OSS-20B and TRIAD architectures. No existing work benchmarks this specific recovery type. (2) POST-HARM RECOVERY: After harm has occurred, the agent must remediate it. BackBench (arXiv 2604.18847, Apr 2026) provides 50 backtracking scenarios in OSWorld for computer-use agents, with a reward model trained on 1,150 pairwise human preference judgments, achieving +120 Elo improvement. This addresses a different problem — harm has already happened and must be undone in GUI/OS environments, not tool-use API settings. (3) POST-INCIDENT RESPONSE: AIR (arXiv 2602.11749, Feb 2026) provides a DSL-based incident response framework for code, embodied, and computer-use agents, achieving >90% detection, remediation, and eradication rates. Critically, AIR terminates the task after remediation and focuses on containing and eradicating incidents — it does not attempt to resume and complete the original task via an alternative safe path. (4) POST-ERROR RECOVERY: RAC (ACM CAIS 2026) provides log-based rollback recovery for general execution errors on tau-bench/REALM-Bench. Fission-GRPO (Jan 2026) trains agents to recover from tool-calling errors via on-policy error augmentation, improving recovery rate by 5.7% on BFCL v4. Hell or High Water (COLM 2025) evaluates recovery from environmental failures. None target safety-specific recovery. Additional relevant concurrent work: SafePred (Feb 2026) achieves 97.6% safety via predictive prevention with world models — prevents unsafe actions but does not address recovery. MOSAIC (Mar 2026) introduces Plan-Check-Act/Refuse with up to 50% harmful behavior reduction — evaluates refusal quality, not post-refusal replanning. SafeAgent (Apr 2026) mentions constrained replanning as a recovery mechanism but provides no disaggregated metrics for replanning success rate, recovery rate, or path quality — overall evaluation uses ASR and NRP without isolating replanning contribution. Mind the GAP (Feb 2026) demonstrates text safety does not transfer to tool-call safety, motivating tool-level guardrails. OpenAgentSafety (ICLR 2026) provides a comprehensive 350+ task evaluation framework for agent safety with real tools but focuses on risk evaluation, not recovery. ATBench (Apr 2026) benchmarks trajectory-level safety with 1,000 trajectories across 2,084 tools but evaluates safety detection, not recovery. ToolSafe (Jan 2026) guides agents toward safety-aware reasoning via pre-execution feedback (TS-Flow), reducing harmful tool invocations by 65% — closest to our setting in spirit, but operates as a guardrail that provides preventive guidance rather than training agents to recover after blocking. TraceSafe (Apr 2026) reveals guardrail efficacy depends more on structural JSON parsing than semantic alignment, suggesting recovery requires structured training beyond guardrail design. DiaTool-DPO (SIGDIAL 2025, arXiv Apr 2025) applies multi-turn DPO to tool-augmented LLMs for dialogue control but does not target safety recovery. Fission-GRPO's on-policy error augmentation mechanism directly inspires our training approach, adapted from general error recovery to safety-specific guardrail recovery. Pattern: 'complementary gap-filling' — rather than claiming to replace existing recovery frameworks, we identify and fill the specific gap where guardrails succeed at blocking but agents fail at task completion.",
  "approach": "We construct RecoverBench by instrumenting tau-bench (Airline + Retail) with a guardrail intervention simulator that injects safety blocks at systematically varied trajectory points, measuring three metrics: Safe Recovery Rate (SRR: percentage of blocked episodes where the agent finds an alternative safe path to task completion), Recovery Latency (additional turns required after blocking), and Alternative Path Quality (semantic similarity to optimal safe trajectories plus task reward preservation). ## Reviewer feedback (round 2)
Issues: ["IMPORTANT: 'From Refusal to Recovery' (arXiv 2510.13727, Oct 2025) is the most thematically adjacent work — its title literally describes the refusal-to-recovery transition — but receives only a footnote-level citation. Must be prominently differentiated in the landscape: it modifies the guardrail (co-optimizes monitor + fallback policy) rather than training the agent; it evaluates on simulated driving/e-commerce, not tool-use API settings; it does not propose a recovery-specific benchmark.", "AAAI 2027 primary target (9 weeks) is unrealistic for benchmark+training method+ablations paper. The scope includes: RecoverBench construction with guardrail intervention simulator, RA-FGRPO implementation with Safety Recovery Simulator, training two model sizes, evaluation sweeps across complexity bins, and four ablation comparisons (RA-FGRPO vs GRPO vs DPO vs ToolSafe).", "GAGPO (arXiv 2605.13217, May 13 2026) is only 6 days old and serves as the foundation for turn-level credit assignment in RA-FGRPO. No independent replication or peer review exists yet. Need a fallback credit assignment strategy.", "ToolMisuseBench (arXiv 2604.01508, Apr 2026) — a 6800-task benchmark for tool misuse and recovery with fault injection — is not cited. While it targets operational errors, its benchmark design (deterministic fault injection, recovery quality metrics, budgeted efficiency) is methodologically adjacent and should be acknowledged.", "Safety Recovery Simulator is underspecified: how exactly will it generate 'available safe alternatives'? This is arguably the hardest component — the quality of diagnostic context determines whether RA-FGRPO can generate meaningful recovery training signal.", "Recovery ceiling not addressed: some blocked scenarios may genuinely have NO safe alternative path. The benchmark should explicitly include 'correctly unrecoverable' tasks and measure the false positive rate of recovery attempts (agent tries to complete but violates safety constraints in doing so)."]
Feedback: The core idea is strong and the revision substantially improved the proposal. Five actionable changes for next round: (1) Promote EACL via ARR Aug 3 to primary target (11 weeks), move AAAI to stretch goal — or scope AAAI submission to benchmark-only (RecoverBench) and defer RA-FGRPO training to NAACL extended version. (2) Add a dedicated paragraph differentiating from 'From Refusal to Recovery' (2510.13727): guardrail-side correction vs. agent-side replanning; simulated driving/e-commerce vs. tool-use API; no recovery benchmark vs. RecoverBench's three metrics. (3) Cite ToolMisuseBench (2604.01508) as the operational-error counterpart to your safety-specific recovery benchmark. (4) Propose AT²PO (arXiv 2601.04767) or GTPO (arXiv 2511.14846) as fallback credit assignment methods if GAGPO proves unreliable, since both are more established. (5) Add 'correctly unrecoverable' scenarios to RecoverBench design and define a False Recovery Rate metric (agent claims to complete task safely but actually violates constraints via a different pathway).

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文。
3. **深度思考**：
   - 核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach？
4. **避免表面修订**：如果反复 minor fix 没有实质改进，考虑 major revision 或 pivot。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

1. **如果'已有类似工作'**：搜索并阅读相关论文，明确差异化点
2. **如果'SOTA 过时'**：查看 Papers With Code 排行榜，更新 baseline
3. **如果'可行性有问题'**：搜索类似实验成本和 GitHub 实现
4. **如果'novelty 不足'**：做 3-5 种关键词搜索，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- You have full freedom: minor fix, major revision, or pivot.
- Include a "change_type" field: "minor", "major", or "pivot".
- Output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields.

**AT²PO: Agentic Turn-based Policy Optimization via Tree Search**

The paper presents a unified framework for multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning.

AT²PO employs a "turn-level tree structure" that jointly supports:

The paper evaluates across **seven benchmarks**, though specific names aren't detailed in the abstract provided.

- Enables sparse credit assignment through turn-wise mechanisms
- Aligns policy optimization with natural agent decision granularity
- Orthogonal design allows integration into existing RL pipelines

**(1) Title & Method:**
"Empowering Multi-Turn Tool-Integrated Agentic Reasoning with Group Turn Policy Optimization" - a reinforcement learning algorithm designed specifically for training LLMs on multi-turn Tool-Integrated Reasoning tasks.

**(2) Credit Assignment Mechanism:**
The method employs "return-based advantage estimation where normalized discounted returns are calculated as advantages," providing a more direct connection between model actions and outcomes.

**(3) Turn-Level Reward Handling:**
GTPO introduces "turn-level reward assignment that provides fine-grained feedback for individual turns" alongside "self-supervised reward shaping that exploits self-supervision signals from generated code to densify sparse binary outcome-based rewards."

**(4) Environments & Benchmarks:**
Math reasoning benchmarks, commonsense reasoning tasks, and program synthesis problems.

**(5) Key Results:**
The approach "outperforms GRPO by 3.0% across diverse math reasoning benchmarks" with "negligible overhead."

**(6) Comparison to GRPO:**
GTPO addresses GRPO's limitation of "coarse-grained, trajectory-level rewards that provide insufficient learning signals," advancing improvement by 3.9% on commonsense reasoning and synthesis tasks.

**(7) Peer Review Status:**
The paper is an arXiv preprint (submitted November 2025, revised April 2026) with no mention of venue acceptance in the provided content.

**(8) Multi-Turn Training Advantages:**
Enables fine-grained feedback at each reasoning step rather than final trajectory-level signals, reducing training stagnation in complex iterative interactions.

Safety for AI systems is about preempting downstream hazards like financial or physical harm. Most AI guardrails rely on output classification based on labeled datasets, making them brittle to new hazardous situations. # ToolMisuseBench: Comprehensive Details

## (1) Fault Injection Taxonomy
The benchmark supports five fault types: "schema drift, rate limit, timeout, authorization related failures, and adversarial error rewriting." These faults isolate failures at "call construction, policy handling, or recovery" stages.

## (2) Recovery Quality Metric
Recovery success measures whether agents can correct and eventually succeed after receiving structured failure feedback. The document tracks "recovery success" as a separate metric from initial task success, showing agents' ability to repair errors.

## (3) Budgeted Efficiency Metric
Budgeted success is computed as: "S(k)=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁ᴺ 𝟙[TaskSuccessᵢ=1∧ToolCallsUsedᵢ≤k]" where N is task count and k is a tool call cap. Area under the curve summarizes "efficiency aware performance."

## (4) "Authorization" and "Hard Failure" Settings
These represent failure scenarios where "baselines remain at zero measured success." Authorization failures involve "policy rule violations," while hard failures include persistent rate limiting—both resist simple repair approaches.

## (5) Schema-Aware vs. Schema-Unaware Methods
Schema repair methods add "repair for common argument errors," while policy-aware baselines add "a lightweight policy awareness layer." The heuristic baseline uses neither enhancement, serving as the unaware baseline.

## (6) Evaluated Models & Performance
Three baselines tested on 1,000 public test tasks:
- **Heuristic**: 0.250 success, 0.000 recovery, 2.95 avg calls
- **Schema repair**: 0.250 success, 0.250 recovery, 3.25 avg calls  
- **Policy-aware**: 0.250 success, 0.250 recovery, 3.25 avg calls

## (7) Safety-Specific Recovery
The benchmark measures operational reliability under "policy violations" and "invalid call behavior," treating safety as enforcement constraints rather than semantic safety (like harmful outputs).

## (8) Declarative Fault Plan Format
Fault plans are "per task and replayed deterministically" with triggers including "tool targeting, nth call targeting, argument pattern targeting, and seeded probabilistic activation."

## (9) Task Generation
Tasks include "instruction, tool schemas, initial state, success criteria, fault plan, and budget limits." The dataset (6,800 tasks) balances domains across CRUD, retrieval, files, and scheduling with enforced coherence validation.

## (10) Connection to Safety Guardrails
The work references "policy first" infrastructure, citing that "explicit enforcement layers around tool orchestration" may be more effective than model-only mitigation. However, this is operational safety, not AI alignment safety.

# Control-Theoretic AI Guardrails: Comprehensive Technical Summary

## 1. Control-Theoretic Formulation

**Safety Value Function**: The framework computes V(z₀^AI) = max_π^AI (min_{t≥0} ℓ_ℱ(s_t)), representing "the closest the AI agent ever gets to failure." The safety margin ℓ_ℱ encodes distance to failure in outcome space (e.g., bank balance above threshold, distance to obstacles).

**Monitor & Recovery**: The approach jointly derives three components:
- Monitor Δ: Evaluates if actions preserve safety using Q-values
- Fallback Policy π_safe: Generates corrective actions when monitoring detects danger
- Intervention Scheme: Switches to recovery policy when Q(z,a) ≤ 0

The monitor uses "a value function that classifies states from which the system cannot avoid failure."

## 2. Fallback Policy Mechanism

The guardrail operates as an external safety filter. When monitoring detects unsafe actions, it injects corrected actions: φ(z,a) returns either the proposed action (if safe) or the fallback policy's action (if unsafe). Importantly, the agent doesn't replan—the guardrail directly modifies generations.

## 3. Recovery Process

During recovery, "the guardrail intervenes at times where the fallback policy has time to correct the base LLM agent away from failures." Recovery doesn't replace the entire action; rather, it substitutes the LLM's unsafe output with a safe alternative from the learned recovery policy at runtime.

## 4. Environment Details

**Agentic Driving**: Vehicle navigates through 2 circular obstacles (radius 0.5m) in a 3m-wide track. Safety margin is minimum distance to obstacles or boundaries.

**Agentic Commerce**: Shopping simulation with cart items; safety requires keeping total under $50 budget with 5-item removal limit before checkout.

**Backseat AI Driver**: LLM provides text advice to human proxy; human follows advice based on perceived urgency.

## 5. Comparison to Simple Refusal

Refusal-based guardrails ("simply refuse to act") prove ineffective in sequential environments: "an AI agent that refuses to steer a self-driving car when approaching an obstacle at high speed can cause an accident through inaction." ReGuard maintains higher success rates (77.3% vs. 44.4% for myopic refusal) while preserving task efficiency.

## 6. Critical Limitation: Simulator Requirement

The authors explicitly acknowledge: "Our approach assumes access to simulators that provide reliable safety outcome signals during training, which remains an open challenge for many agentic domains."

## 7. Guardrail Independence

The guardrail is **purely external and model-agnostic**—"the same guardrail can shield multiple LLM agents without access to their weights or training data." It doesn't co-optimize with the base agent; it monitors and corrects post-generation.

## 8. Safety-Critical RL Training Recipe

Training uses DDQN (Double Deep Q-Learning) on discounted safety Bellman: Q(z,a) = (1-γ)ℓ_ℱ(s₊) + γ min{ℓ_ℱ(s₊), max_a Q(z₊,a)}. The vocabulary is constrained to top-p tokens from the base model (p=0.9) to maintain coherence while optimizing safety objectives.

## 9. Multi-Step Agentic Settings

ReGuard demonstrates effectiveness across multi-turn interactions: e-commerce requires planning 5 steps ahead for removal ordering; backseat driving involves human-AI loops across trajectories. The framework explicitly handles "the evolving sequence of actions and their downstream consequences on the world."

## 10. Baseline Comparisons

- **Privileged**: Upper bound assuming true world state access
- **ZeroShot models**: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B (prompting to act as safety filters)
- **LlamaGuard**: Supervised text classifier for safety
- **Myopic baselines**: Single-step safety judgments with recovery policies
- **Human proxy**: Simulated user following AI advice (backseat driving)

ReGuard achieved 77.3% success (vs. 23.4% for ZeroShot baselines) and 0.99 value F1 score in driving, demonstrating that "consequence-aware guardrails trained on downstream outcomes are more reliable monitors than today's proxy-based guardrails."

# GAGPO Technical Details Extraction

## 1. Grouped Value Proxy Formulation

Groups are formed by collecting all trajectory steps with identical environment states: **"𝒢(s)={(i,t)∣s^(i)_t=s}"**. The non-parametric proxy averages discounted returns across same-state occurrences: **"V̄(s)=1/|𝒢(s)| ∑_(j,u)∈𝒢(s) R̂^(j)_u"**

## 2. TD/GAE-Style Advantage (No Critic)

The temporal-difference residual is: **"δ^(i)_t = r^(i)_t + γV̄(s^(i)_{t+1}) - V̄(s^(i)_t)"**

Step-level advantages follow recursively: **"Â^(i)_t = δ^(i)_t + γλÂ^(i)_{t+1}"**, equivalent to **"∑^(T_i-t)_{l=0}(γλ)^l δ^(i)_{t+l}"**

## 3. Rollout Grouping Mechanism

In text-based environments (ALFWorld, WebShop), identical states are identified via **"exact textual match"** across collected trajectories. The paper acknowledges this approach limits applicability to deterministic, text-based observations.

## 4. Multi-Turn Tool-Calling Agents

The paper doesn't explicitly address tool-calling agents. It focuses on LLM agents in household task simulation and e-commerce environments, treating each environment step as the credit assignment unit rather than individual tokens.

## 5. Performance: Exact Numbers vs Baselines

**ALFWorld (Qwen2.5-1.5B):**
- GAGPO: 93.5±1.3 vs GiGPO: 88.1±1.95
- Gain: +5.4 points

**WebShop (Qwen2.5-1.5B):**
- GAGPO score: 88.6±3.3 vs GiGPO: 79.8±1.2 (+8.8)
- GAGPO success: 78.1±1.1 vs GiGPO: 62.5±1.1 (+15.6 points)

**7B model shows similar improvements** (+6.8 ALFWorld, +4.0 WebShop score points)

## 6. Comparison to GRPO/PPO/TTPO

GAGPO outperforms GRPO and PPO across both benchmarks. The paper doesn't directly compare TTPO (Turn-PPO), though it cites Turn-PPO as using auxiliary critics for step-level feedback, whereas GAGPO remains critic-free.

## 7. Group-Normalized PPO Update

Advantages are standardized within rollout groups: **"A^(i)_t = (Â^(i)_t - μ_ℬ)/(σ_ℬ + ϵ)"** where μ_ℬ, σ_ℬ are group statistics. A length-normalized action sequence importance ratio replaces token-level clipping, maintaining step-level advantage assignments across all tokens in an action.

## 8. Limitations Mentioned

- **Exact state matching requirement**: Groups shrink to singleton size in stochastic or partially observable environments
- **Evaluation scope**: Only sparse episode-end rewards tested; no dense reward or continuous action settings studied
- **Safety concerns**: Deployment risks with autonomous agents in open environments

## 9. Computational Overhead vs GRPO

Not explicitly quantified. GAGPO adds non-parametric value proxy construction and group-wise normalization but avoids maintaining separate critic networks.

## 10. Step-Aligned vs Turn-Level Credit (vs TTPO)

GAGPO applies temporal credit recursion at environment **steps** with grouped value bootstrapping. Turn-PPO uses auxiliary value models for turn-level estimation. GAGPO achieves similar precision through non-parametric grouping without learned value functions.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about τ²-bench (tau2-bench):

## Overview

τ²-bench is a benchmark for evaluating conversational agents in dual-control environments where both agent and user actively use tools to modify shared state.

## Key Contributions

The benchmark introduces four key contributions: 1) A novel Telecom dual-control domain modeled as a Dec-POMDP, where both agent and user make use of tools to act in a shared, dynamic environment that tests both agent coordination and communication, 2) A compositional task generator that programmatically creates diverse, verifiable tasks from atomic components, ensuring domain coverage and controlled complexity, 3) A reliable user simulator tightly coupled with the environment, whose behavior is constrained by tools and observable states, improving simulation fidelity, 4) Fine-grained analysis of agent performance through multiple ablations including separating errors arising from reasoning vs communication/coordination.

## Motivation

Existing benchmarks for conversational AI agents simulate single-control environments, where only the AI agent can use tools to interact with the world, while the user remains a passive information provider. This differs from real-world scenarios like technical support, where users need to actively participate in modifying the state of the (shared) world.

## Performance Findings

Experiments show significant performance drops when agents shift from no-user to dual-control, highlighting the challenges of guiding users.

# AT²PO: Complete Technical Breakdown

## (1) Seven Evaluation Benchmarks

**Multi-Hop QA (4):** HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle

**Single-Hop QA (3):** Natural Questions (NQ), TriviaQA, PopQA

## (2) Performance Numbers (Qwen3-4B results)

| Method | HotpotQA | 2Wiki | MuSiQue | Bamboogle | NQ | TriviaQA | PopQA | Avg |
|--------|----------|-------|---------|-----------|-----|----------|-------|------|
| ReAct | 30.42 | 32.92 | 12.83 | 44.80 | 30.01 | 26.75 | 53.53 | 35.34 |
| GRPO | 44.76 | 51.40 | 21.60 | 50.40 | 46.02 | 45.98 | 65.17 | 49.18 |
| DAPO | 45.95 | 51.81 | 21.68 | 51.20 | 46.65 | 47.50 | 65.84 | 51.03 |
| GSPO | 47.07 | 49.25 | 22.68 | 50.40 | 45.69 | 46.01 | 64.24 | 48.50 |
| AEPO | 46.36 | 51.78 | 23.47 | 50.40 | 46.95 | 45.71 | 64.66 | 50.13 |
| **AT²PO** | **49.44** | **52.99** | **24.80** | **54.4** | **48.81** | **47.90** | **65.32** | **56.44** |

**Key finding:** AT²PO achieved gains "up to 1.84 percentage points in average over the state-of-the-art baseline."

## (3) Turn-wise Credit Assignment Formula

The document presents a recursive value propagation mechanism:

```
Vₙ = {
  r̂ₙ,                          if n is leaf
  Σ(c∈C(n)) wc·Vc,            otherwise
}

where wc = Hπθ(c) / Σ(c'∈C(n))Hπθ(c')
```

Child nodes weighted by entropy; "recursively aggregates to propagate outcome-based rewards backward through the tree." Advantages computed as A_n = V_n.

## (4) Entropy-Guided Tree Expansion Mechanism

**Phase 1 - Initialization:** Generate M independent trajectories per prompt; build trees with all state-action pairs.

**Phase 2 - Iterative Expansion:** For L iterations:
- Score non-leaf nodes: s(n) = H_πθ(n) - α|children(n.parent)|
- Select top-K highest-entropy nodes with branching penalty coefficient α
- Regenerate continuations from selected nodes

Result: M + LK leaf nodes per prompt. The paper states this "generates a larger number of diverse rollouts under the same computational budget."

## (5) Turn-Level Policy Optimization Objective

```
JATPO(θ) = E[1/G Σᵢ 1/|yᵢ| Σₜ Mᵢ,ₜ min(sᵢ,ₜᵗᵘʳⁿ(θ)Âᵢ,ₜ, 
            clip(sᵢ,ₜᵗᵘʳⁿ(θ), 1-εₗ, 1+εᵣ)Âᵢ,ₜ)]
```

Turn-level importance ratio combines token-level gradient with turn-sequence ratio using stop-gradient operations. Distinguishes from token-level (high variance) and sequence-level (coarse) approaches.

## (6) Computational Overhead

The paper acknowledges: "tree-based expansion introduces additional computational overhead compared to linear rollouts, particularly when sufficient computational resources are available."

Configuration used: M=10, L=2, K=6 (10 initial branches + 2 expansion iterations × 6 nodes = 22 total leaves). Token budget approximately (M+LK/2)·B where B is individual rollout length. DAPO uses 3× rollout budget but achieved comparable results with equal budgets.

## (7) LLM Backbone Models

- Qwen3-4B
- Qwen3-8B  
- Qwen2.5-7B

All experiments conducted on "8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs."

## (8) Comparison to GRPO

AT²PO vs GRPO on Qwen3-4B multi-hop average: 48.81% vs 45.42% (3.39 point improvement). 

Key differences: GRPO operates at token-level with "individual importance sampling ratios" causing high variance. AT²PO's turn-level formulation reduces "clipped tokens and improves training stability." Ablation study shows replacing random tree search with ATPO loss yielded "substantial gains across all multi-hop benchmarks."

## (9) Tool-Use/API-Call Benchmarks

All seven benchmarks integrate Wikipedia search tool calling. Document specifies: "agents act through turns of interleaved thinking and tool use, with tool responses forming subsequent observations." Maximum tool-calls capped at 6 per trajectory. Uses e5-base-v2 retriever on 21-million-entry Wikipedia corpus returning top-3 passages per query.

## (10) Stated Limitations

Direct quote: "tree-based expansion introduces additional computational overhead...particularly when sufficient computational resources are available, as the expansion process requires multiple sequential iterations."

Additionally: aim to "evaluate AT2PO in a broader range of agentic environments to further assess its generalization and robustness." Training stability issues observed with Tree-GRPO baseline (Appendix C) attributed to "retokenization drift."

The paper with arXiv ID 2603.19328 is titled "The Verifier Tax: Horizon Dependent Safety Success Tradeoffs in Tool Using LLM Agents."

**Key Findings:**

The research studies how runtime enforcement against unsafe actions affects end-to-end task performance in multi-step tool using LLM agents, using tau-bench across Airline and Retail domains to compare baseline Tool-Calling, planning-integrated (TRIAD), and policy-mediated (TRIAD-SAFETY) architectures with GPT-OSS-20B and GLM-4-9B.

The researchers identified model dependent interaction horizons (15 to 30 turns) and decomposed outcomes into overall success rate (SR), safe success rate (SSR), and unsafe success rate (USR).

The results reveal a persistent Safety Capability Gap—while safety mediation can intercept up to 94 percent of non-compliant actions, it rarely translates into strictly safe goal attainment (SSR below 5 percent in most settings).

The paper proposes the "Verifier Tax" on operational overhead (2.0–2.8× token inflation across all model×domain settings) and proposes Strict Grounding Gates to mitigate integrity leaks.

## Overview

AgentSpec, accepted at ICSE 2026, introduces a customizable runtime enforcement framework with a rule-based DSL for specifying safety properties of LLM agents.

## Core Approach

AgentSpec is a lightweight domain-specific language for specifying and enforcing runtime constraints on LLM agents, where users define structured rules that incorporate triggers, predicates, and enforcement mechanisms, ensuring agents operate within predefined safety boundaries.

An AgentSpec rule is represented as a three-tuple consisting of a triggering event, a set of predicate functions, and a sequence of enforcement functions.

AgentSpec is implemented across multiple domains, including code execution, embodied agents, and autonomous driving, demonstrating its adaptability and effectiveness. AgentSpec supports both preventive and corrective enforcement modes and evaluates on WebArena and ToolEmu benchmarks.

## Overview

SafeAgentBench is a new benchmark for safety-aware task planning of embodied LLM agents. SafeAgentBench includes a dataset with 750 tasks, covering 10 potential hazards and 3 task types, as well as SafeAgentEnv (a universal embodied environment) and reliable evaluation methods from both execution and semantic perspectives.

## Dataset Composition

The dataset consists of 450 tasks with various safety hazard issues and 300 corresponding safe tasks as a control group, covering 10 common risks to humans and property, and includes three distinct categories of tasks: detailed tasks, abstract tasks, and long-horizon tasks.

## Evaluation Metrics and Refusal Rates

The benchmark uses 5 metrics to evaluate agent performance: rejection rate, risk/success rate (goal), risk/success rate (LLM), execution rate and usage time, with rejection rate indicating tasks an agent refuses and reflecting its proactive safety awareness.
